payload.name: Extract explicit advice as memories
payload.description: When a speaker gives explicit advice, recommendations, or instructions to another person about how to do something, during extraction, create a memory capturing the advice and its topic.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly advises, recommends, or instructs another person on how to do or decide something, create a memory that captures the advice (what was recommended) and the target activity or decision. Use a memory type that fits the fact (e.g., relationship, preference, or event). Do not skip such statements merely because they are short or embedded in a longer exchange.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that the construction agent processed a message containing explicit advice but failed to extract any candidate, so the advice was never persisted. The reusable rule is to treat explicit advice or recommendations from one speaker to another as extraction candidates regardless of the surrounding topic. This applies to any future conversation where a user offers guidance on how to do something and a downstream question may ask about that advice.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Belief-Advice Statements During Ingestion
payload.description: When a participant explicitly tells another what to believe or how to value themselves, extract it as a memory candidate even in supportive/emotional dialogue.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly states a belief, value, or guidance they want another participant to adopt (e.g., 'Your worth is not defined by your weight'), create a memory candidate capturing that claim.
Do not ignore such statements because they appear only in encouragement, reassurance, or advice; treat them as durable facts about the speaker's message to the recipient.

When the claim is a directive about self-worth, priorities, or principles, prefer storing it as a preference of the speaker or a state/relationship memory for the recipient, following the session context.

candidates.solves: When a participant explicitly tells another what to believe or how to think about themselves, extraction often overlooks it because the statement is phrased as supportive advice rather than a factual event. This skill ensures such belief-advice statements become memory candidates so future questions about the guidance can be answered from the persisted session. It applies during ingestion of any dialogue where one participant prescribes a value or self-perception to another, but not to mere factual updates or off-topic small talk.

payload.name: PreserveExplicitAttributedValuesSeparately
payload.description: When a message explicitly attributes a value, lesson, or advice to a specific person and the speaker indicates a future intention to follow it, extract that as its own focused memory instead of folding it into a broad conversation summary.
content: During extraction, if a message explicitly states that a specific person stressed or taught a value and the speaker says they want to keep it in mind, create a separate memory capturing that specific value and the person who stressed it, rather than only creating a broad event summary of the conversation.

Before merging into an existing general memory, check that this explicit value/attribution is preserved as its own claim; if the existing memory lacks it, add or update a dedicated memory with the specific value and the person who stressed it.

candidates.solves: Construction fails when a message contains an explicit attribution of a value/lesson to a specific person plus the speaker's stated intent to apply it, because one broad conversation summary omits that durable claim. This rule applies during extraction/CRUD whenever such explicit attributed values occur; it does not apply to general conversation summaries with no explicit attribution.

payload.name: ExtractExplicitFutureGoalsAndAspirations
payload.description: When a message contains an explicit statement about what the speaker wants to do or achieve in the future, extract it as a memory candidate during extraction.
content: During extraction, treat explicit future intentions, goals, or aspirations stated by the speaker as extractable memories, even when they describe long-term or post-career plans; do not skip such messages merely because they are reflective.
Represent each stated aspiration as a plan or state candidate tied to the speaker, recording the desired outcome and any optional actions, and link it to the source message.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that a clear statement of future intentions was ingested but no memory candidate was extracted, causing silent data loss. The reusable mechanism is omission of explicit future goals or aspirations during extraction. A skill that forces extraction of stated plans and desired outcomes transfers across any future-oriented intention statements, preventing the same ingestion-stage loss.

payload.name: Preserve_Explicit_Advice_During_Extraction
payload.description: When extracting memory candidates, preserve explicit advice, recommendations, or instructions in content instead of summarizing a mixed message as generic support; use when a speaker gives concrete guidance alongside encouragement.
content: During candidate extraction, if a source message contains explicit advice, recommendations, or action steps, include that specific guidance in the candidate content; do not reduce the message to a generic emotional-support summary.
When a message mixes concrete instructions with encouragement, prioritize the actionable content so a future recall can retrieve what was advised, not just that support was offered.
When updating an existing memory, ensure the new content preserves or merges any concrete advice from the source and does not become more generic than the previous version.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: an extraction candidate reduced a message containing concrete advice to a generic summary of encouragement, so future questions about the advice cannot be answered. The reusable mechanism is collapsing actionable guidance into vague support during memory extraction. This applies to any conversational message where a speaker gives explicit recommendations alongside emotional support; the skill ensures those recommendations are preserved in memory content.

payload.name: Extract explicit future plans as distinct memories
payload.description: When constructing memories, if a speaker states a future plan or joke in one message, ensure it is extracted as a distinct candidate and not merged with unrelated earlier statements from other turns.
content: During extraction, if a message contains an explicit future intention, plan, or joke (e.g., 'Maybe I'll...', 'I might...'), extract it as its own candidate, preserving the specific activity and using memory_kind 'plan' for intentions or 'event' for jokes/hypotheticals.

Do not merge this statement with earlier unrelated reflections about the speaker's habits or thoughts; keep candidates scoped to the source message unless the content is explicitly connected by the speaker.
When in doubt, prefer a separate candidate over an incomplete merged one; a longer, accurate memory is better than a short one that omits a key claim.

candidates.solves: The failure occurred because the extraction candidate merged a speaker's explicit future plan (writing a screenplay) with unrelated earlier reflections, omitting the plan. The generalizable mechanism is that extraction can conflate content across turns and drop key stated intentions. This skill applies whenever a message contains an explicit future intention or hypothetical activity; it directs the agent to keep such statements as separate, faithful memory candidates.

payload.name: Extract direct suggestions as memory candidates
payload.description: When a conversation contains a direct suggestion, recommendation, or encouragement from one speaker to another (e.g. 'Keep doing X', 'try Y'), use this skill during memory construction to ensure that advice is captured as a candidate and not skipped as non-factual.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit advice or suggestions as memory-worthy. If a speaker directly tells another participant to continue, try, or adopt an action ('Keep doing X', 'You should Y', 'Try Z'), do not skip the message because it is not a statement of current fact.

Record the speaker, the addressee, and the recommended action in the candidate (e.g., as a state or event memory). During CRUD, preserve such candidates as normal memory updates and do not discard them for being advice.

candidates.solves: Memory construction misses explicit suggestions and advice phrased as encouragement or second-person guidance, leaving later questions about recommendations unanswerable. The failure mechanism is skipping non-assertive speech acts during candidate extraction. This skill applies whenever one speaker directly tells another to keep doing, try, or adopt an action, and requires capturing that advice as a candidate.

payload.name: Extract Encouragement and Supportive Utterances
payload.description: When a speaker offers encouragement, sympathy, advice, or reassurance to another person, extract it as an event or relationship memory, including the key content and any linked setback.
content: During extraction, treat supportive, encouraging, or advising messages as memory-worthy events: record the speaker, the recipient, and the gist of the support/advice (e.g., 'X told Y that rejections don't define her, keep trying').
If the support references a prior setback or difficulty (explicit or implied), link this event to that existing state/event memory.
Also evaluate whether the utterance reveals a relationship quality (e.g., supportive, caring) and update or create a relationship memory between the participants when appropriate.

candidates.solves: The Construction Agent sometimes fails to extract memories from messages that contain emotional support, encouragement, or advice, leaving such facts unpersisted and unanswerable later. This occurs because supportive utterances are not explicitly recognized as memory-worthy events or relationship cues. This skill applies whenever one participant offers reassurance, motivation, or guidance to another, especially after a setback or challenge, and guides extraction of the gist, the relationship signal, and any linked prior state.

payload.name: Extract suggestions and recommendations
payload.description: When a message contains one participant explicitly suggesting or recommending a specific item, resource, activity, or action to another participant, extract it as a memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, when a speaker explicitly suggests or recommends a specific item (e.g., a book, resource, activity, action) to another participant, create a memory capturing the suggestion. Include the suggested item and the stated purpose or benefit if present. Store it as an event or relationship memory, evidence-bound and source-linked to the message. Do not skip such statements because they are phrased as advice rather than assertions.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an explicit suggestion or recommendation made by one participant to another was not extracted during candidate ingestion, leaving a gap for later questions about what someone suggested. The failure mechanism is a tendency to skip advisory statements as non-factual. A reusable rule to extract suggestions as event or relationship memories applies to any future conversation with explicit recommendations of items, resources, or actions, independent of topic.

payload.name: ExtractAdviceSuggestionsFromConversation
payload.description: When a speaker offers a suggestion, recommendation, or advice to another participant, use this skill to extract it as a memory candidate even if embedded or not accepted.
content: During candidate extraction, identify turns where one speaker advises, recommends, or suggests an action to another (e.g., 'consider X', 'maybe try Y'). Create a memory candidate for the suggestion even if it is part of a longer message and regardless of whether the recipient accepts it.

When storing the suggestion, prefer a 'plan' memory type if the suggested action is intended for the recipient; otherwise use 'preference' if it reflects the advisor's own preference. Record the advisor, recipient, and the advised action.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: extraction missed a suggestion because it was embedded in a longer message and not accepted. The abstract mechanism is that advisory statements, especially those referring to a prior problem, are often not captured. This skill applies to future conversations where a participant gives a recommendation or advice to another; it does not apply to purely factual statements or exchanges without advisory intent.

payload.name: Preserve explicit process steps in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a message that describes how to do something (care, maintenance, routine, procedure), preserve each concrete step/action in memory content; do not reduce the message to an evaluative summary or preference.
content: During extraction, if a message answers a how-to or process question by listing concrete actions (e.g., keep clean, feed properly, provide light), capture those actions as part of the memory content, not just an overall judgment like 'low-maintenance'.

When a speaker expresses an attitude about a task and then gives enumerated steps, extract the steps as separate factual details or include them explicitly in the same memory; the evaluative label alone is insufficient.
Use memory_kind and subject appropriate to the speaker; the concrete steps belong in the content regardless of whether they are framed as preference or routine.

candidates.solves: When a speaker answers a how-to or process question with an evaluative statement plus concrete steps (e.g., 'not tough; do X, do Y'), extraction often keeps only the evaluation and drops the steps. This skill requires preserving all explicit procedural steps in memory so later factual questions about the process can be answered.

payload.name: ExtractPlansFromInvitationReplies
payload.description: During extraction, use when a speaker replies to an invitation or question about future plans with concrete desired activities, even if tentative ('maybe we can', 'I'd love to').
content: During candidate extraction, if a speaker responds to an invitation or a question about future plans by naming concrete activities they would like to do, create a plan candidate even if the message has no explicit date or commitment words.

Use 'plan' as the memory type for activities to be done together at a future visit or event; include the participants and the activity, and resolve relative times ('tomorrow', 'when I come over') from the message timestamp.
Do not skip such replies because they are conversational or tentative; 'maybe we can' or 'I'd love to' still expresses an intention worth persisting.

candidates.solves: When a speaker replies to an invitation or a question about upcoming plans by naming concrete activities they would like to do together, the Construction Agent sometimes fails to extract any candidate, so the plan is never persisted. This pattern occurs across any future-visit, meeting, or event dialogue whenever tentative or conversational phrasing still expresses a clear intention. The skill generalizes the need to treat such replies as plan candidates regardless of the specific activity, time, or participants.

payload.name: Verify existing coverage before skipping add candidate
payload.description: When a construction decision is about to SKIP an extracted fact with a reason like 'already included' or 'already in memory', verify against the retrieved memory pool and accepted changes before skipping.
content: Before choosing SKIP for an extracted candidate, verify that the fact is actually covered by a retrieved existing memory or by an earlier accepted ADD/UPDATE in the same batch. If no such memory or change exists, do not skip: ADD the candidate as a new memory.
Do not accept a SKIP reason such as 'Information already included in the updated memory' unless you can identify the specific memory ID or change event that contains the same fact.

candidates.solves: Construction SKIP can drop valid facts when the model assumes prior coverage ('already included') without checking the existing-memory pool or accepted batch changes. Apply whenever a candidate is about to be SKIPped as duplicate: confirm the fact exists in retrieved memories or earlier accepted updates. Not for cases with actual coverage or retrieval-side issues.

payload.name: Verify duplicate before skipping memory candidate
payload.description: When a Construction Agent is about to SKIP an extracted candidate because it appears duplicate, verify an equivalent memory actually exists in the retrieved related-memory pool before skipping. If no such memory is present, do not SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate on duplicate grounds, confirm that an equivalent memory is actually present in the retrieved related-memory pool or current snapshot version.
If no existing memory supports the claimed duplication, do not skip: ADD the candidate, or MERGE only when a concrete target memory exists.
A generic 'duplicate information already represented' reason is not sufficient when the related-memory pool is empty or contains no matching memory.

candidates.solves: During batched memory construction, a candidate can be marked as duplicate and skipped even when the related-memory pool contains no equivalent memory, so the fact is never persisted. This rule ensures duplicate checks compare against actually retrieved existing memories rather than inferred or generic duplication. It applies to future construction decisions where SKIP is considered for a new candidate and no matching memory is visible in the retrieved pool.

payload.name: Verify existing memory before SKIP decision
payload.description: When a construction candidate would be skipped as already represented, verify that a matching memory actually exists in the retrieved existing-memory pool before selecting SKIP; if no matching memory is found, choose ADD.
content: Before applying SKIP to a candidate with the reason 'already represented', explicitly search the retrieved existing-memory pool for a memory that covers the same subject, predicate, and key details.
If no such memory is found in the retrieved pool, do not SKIP the candidate; create it with ADD (or MERGE/UPDATE only if a partially related memory exists).
SKIP is only valid when the exact fact is demonstrably present in the visible memory pool; absence of the fact is not a reason to discard the candidate.

candidates.solves: Construction decisions sometimes skip adding a candidate because they assume the fact already exists in memory, even when the retrieved existing-memory pool contains no matching memory. This causes durable facts to be lost. The fix is a reusable rule: before choosing SKIP on the grounds that a candidate is already represented, the agent must confirm the matching memory is actually present in the retrieved pool; if it is absent, ADD the candidate. This applies to any future construction batch where a candidate seems redundant but the pool does not contain the corresponding memory.

payload.name: Verify actual redundancy before skipping candidate
payload.description: Use when deciding to SKIP a candidate as duplicate or redundant; if the related memory pool is empty or lacks the equivalent fact, persist the candidate instead.
content: Before skipping a candidate with reason 'duplicate or redundant', verify that a retrieved related memory explicitly contains the same subject and fact; an empty pool or a non-covering memory invalidates the skip.

When the related memory pool is empty or does not contain the equivalent fact, ADD the candidate (or MERGE into the closest existing memory if the fact is missing there) rather than skipping it. When uncertain, prefer persisting over dropping evidence.

candidates.solves: Construction sessions sometimes skip an ADD candidate as 'duplicate or redundant' without verifying that a related memory actually covers the fact, which loses evidence when the memory pool is empty. This rule requires confirming redundancy against the retrieved memory set and, when none exists, persisting the candidate to preserve the fact.

payload.name: Verify duplicate before SKIP in construction
payload.description: When a construction candidate is marked as a duplicate but no retrieved existing memory matches its subject and content, use this to require verification before SKIP.
content: Before choosing SKIP for a candidate, confirm that an actually retrieved existing memory contains the same subject and fact; never assume duplication from prior conversation or memory. If the existing-memory pool has no matching memory, ADD the candidate as a new memory with the appropriate kind and source link.

candidates.solves: Prevents construction from dropping valid extracted facts by SKIPping them as duplicates when no retrieved existing memory actually contains the same information. Applies whenever a candidate is skipped on duplication grounds and the existing-memory pool is empty or lacks a matching memory.

payload.name: AddNewMemoryWhenNoExistingMatch
payload.description: When a candidate contains new, evidence-backed information and no existing memory is retrieved for merging, use ADD rather than SKIP.
content: During CRUD decisions, if no existing memory matches a candidate, do not skip it for that reason; issue an ADD operation to create a new memory.
Before deciding SKIP, confirm the candidate is redundant or unsupported; lack of an update/merge target alone is not a valid skip reason.
This applies to the CRUD decision stage; extraction should still produce candidates for all new facts regardless of existing memory.

candidates.solves: This addresses the pattern where a new, evidence-backed fact is dropped during CRUD because no existing memory matches. The rule applies to any candidate representing new information; it does not apply when the candidate is redundant, unsupported, or outside the allowed memory kinds.

payload.name: Verify Existing Memory Before Skip Already Included
payload.description: Use during construction CRUD decisions when a candidate is marked SKIP with the reason 'already included in the updated memory' or similar. Before skipping, confirm that a prior memory version or the current pool actually contains the fact; otherwise ADD the candidate.
content: Before deciding SKIP on an ADD candidate with reason 'already included in updated memory', check the retrieved existing-memory pool and prior versions for the same subject and fact. If no memory contains that information, do not skip; perform ADD to persist the extracted fact. Only SKIP when you can point to an existing memory version that genuinely includes the fact.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes skip a newly extracted fact as 'already included' even when no prior memory contains it, losing durable facts. The reusable rule is to verify the fact exists in the retrieved pool or prior versions before SKIPing for duplication; if not, ADD the candidate. Applies to any future construction CRUD decision where a SKIP reason claims existing coverage but no memory supports it.

payload.name: Confirm-Duplicate-Before-Skip
payload.description: Apply during construction when a memory candidate would be SKIPped because the information is already included; verify a real memory exists first.
content: Before choosing SKIP with reason 'information already included', identify the exact memory that already contains the candidate's fact: either an existing memory from the retrieved pool or a memory actually created earlier in the same batch.
If no such memory exists, do not SKIP the candidate; ADD it as a new memory.
When multiple candidates in the same batch are near-duplicates, create at least one memory from them instead of skipping all of them with the assumption that another candidate will be persisted.

candidates.solves: Construction agents sometimes SKIP a memory candidate with the reason 'information already included' even when no prior memory exists and no memory is actually created, causing the fact to be lost. This Skill applies whenever a candidate is dismissed as a duplicate: it requires confirming a concrete existing or newly created memory before skipping, and otherwise forces an ADD. It generalizes to any CRUD decision where redundancy is assumed without evidence.
